newsitem.title: CHINA: Australia pledges human rights aid to China.
newsitem.headline: Australia pledges human rights aid to China.

text.p: Australia said on Thursday it had pledged an aid package to help improve human rights in China after a landmark dialogue on the thorny issue with Beijing.

Canberra would spend A$300,000 ($222,000) on a plan to help conduct research and train personnel in aspects of China's criminal and judicial processes, Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said in a statement.

"The programme will focus on institutional strengthening, policy development, research, training and administrative resources in the human rights field," Downer said in the statement given to reporters in Beijing.
The aid was agreed on during unprecedented talks on human rights between Chinese officials and an Australian delegation.
China agreed to the dialogue after Canberra decided not to back a move in the United Nations to condemn Beijing for human rights abuses.

"I do not believe that it is productive to lecture other countries about human rights, but rather that we aim to work together to achieve practical outcomes which actually improve the lives of individuals," Downer said.

Beijing came under fire at the U.N. Human Rights Commission meeting in Geneva in March and April but escaped formal censure after Australia, France and Germany refused to back a motion critical of China tabled by Denmark.

The eight-member Australian delegation led by Bill Farmer, deputy secretary of foreign affairs, arrived in Beijing on Monday for four days of talks that raised human rights principles as well as individual human rights cases in China, sources close to the talks said.
Many human rights abuses in China stemmed from poor enforcement of laws and from local officials overstepping their authority, said one source, who asked not to be identified.

"They are keen to improve the situation, in particular the observance of their laws...and are prepared to acknowledge that they have problems in observance of those laws, especially in regional areas," the source said.

The delegation had asked the Chinese for information on "quite a number" of people whom Australia believed were victims of human rights abuse in China, the source said, but declined to specify whose cases were raised.
Another source familiar with the talks said the delegation had urged Beijing to allow officials from the International Committee of the Red Cross to inspect Chinese prisons.
"The Chinese confirmed that they will continue to talk to the ICRC about the possibility of a visit, but it's apparent that the matter is not yet resolved," the source said.

Chinese officials had said Beijing would likely sign an international covenant on economic, social and cultural rights before the end of the year and was still considering a second covenant on political and civil rights, the source said.

China rejects international criticisms of its policies on dissent as interference in its internal affairs, arguing that the right to the bare necessities of life is more important than political rights.
Western governments have slammed China for a wide-ranging crackdown on dissent in 1996 that saw almost the entire Chinese pro-democracy movement jailed, intimidated into silence or driven into exile.
